newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat pessimistic over U.S. envoy's mission.
newsitem.headline: Arafat pessimistic over U.S. envoy's mission.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Monday he doubted U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross would bring new ideas to break an Israel-PLO peace deadlock over Jewish settlements.
Ross was due to return to the Middle East on Tuesday, the same day Arafat was scheduled to hold talks with Israeli President Ezer Weizman at the Erez border crossing in Gaza.

The peace process plunged into crisis in March after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave bulldozers the green light to break ground for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on land claimed by Israel and the Palestinians.

Arafat held talks in Cairo on Monday with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and was asked by reporters on his return to Gaza whether he believed Ross was coming with new ideas. "I don't think so," Arafat replied.
The Palestinian leader said Israel was seeking the "Judaisation of Jerusalem" and had failed to implement at least 34 elements of its peace deals with the PLO.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said after the Mubarak-Arafat meeting that the only way to rescue the stalled peace process was to deal directly with Israel's policy of building settlements on disputed Arab land.

"Let us use all of our diplomatic, political power in coordination with Arab countries, the contacts with Europe and the United States in order to save the peace process, open more doors and resist the attempts by certain circles of extremists, in particular in Israel, to close all doors," Moussa told reporters in Cairo.

"Everyone feels the danger of the situation. It cannot be rescued unless the issue of settlements, specifically the settlement policy in East Jerusalem and settlements on all occupied Palestinian land, is dealt with."
"Any movement (by the envoys) must take into consideration the danger of settlements and their negative effect on the peace process," Moussa added.
Arafat said on Sunday that Israel's construction of Jewish settlements was a main issue behind the deadlock in peace talks.
"The Judaisation of Quds (Jerusalem) is a dangerous crime as well as continued action to confiscate land and build settlements, especially Jabal Abu Ghneim," he told reporters.

"This is the basic issue between us and them, in addition to lack of accurate and honest implementation of what has been agreed upon, whether it be the first, second or third peace agreements signed in Washington or Cairo."
On his upcoming meeting with Weizman, whose post is largely ceremonial, Arafat said: "The most important thing that his excellency is interested (is) to help us to save the peace process together."
But Arafat said the Israeli government "is insisting (on) continuing its breaching" of the peace deals.
Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani said settlements remained the key to reviving peace efforts.
"I want to tell (Ross) if he wants to move ahead...if we want the peace process to get back on the right track, we should talk settlements," Kanafani told reporters in Gaza.
"This is the magic word to open the way (for) the peace process," he said.

Netanyahu has vowed to plough ahead with the expansion of settlements Israel has already built on land captured in the 1967 Middle East war. He also has pledged not to stop work at the East Jerusalem site called Jabal Abu Ghneim by Arabs and Har Homa by Israel.
Israel regards East Jerusalem as part of its indivisible capital, Palestinians view it as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
